title: Selection Sort
summary: Build a sorted list by choosing the smallest remaining item. Trace selection sort swaps and compare complete programs in six languages.
introduction: Suppose you arrange four books by height. Find the shortest book and place it first. Then find the shortest book left and place it second. Selection sort follows this choose-and-place plan for numbers.
learningObjectives: Find the smallest item in the unfinished part
Explain why selection sort still scans an ordered list

blocks.text: Selection sort splits the list into a finished left part and an unfinished right part. It searches the unfinished part for the smallest value, then swaps that value into the next finished position.
The smallest variable stores a position, not the smallest number itself. We need the position so we know which two items to swap.

items: Start with [4, 2, 3, 1]. The smallest value in the whole list is 1 at position 3.
Swap positions 0 and 3 to get [1, 2, 3, 4]. Position 0 is now finished.
Scan positions 1 through 3. The smallest value is 2, already at position 1, so the swap leaves it there.
Scan positions 2 through 3. Keep 3 at position 2. The last remaining value, 4, is already in place.

blocks.text: The same program in six languages

Choose the language you are learning. Each tab solves the same problem and prints the same result. JavaScript can run in this page. The other tabs need separate local tools: a C11 compiler, a C++17 compiler, Python 3, .NET 8 or later for C#, or Java 17. Use Program.cs for C# and Main.java for Java.
The output is the sorted list. Although the first swap happens to order this example completely, the remaining scans still run. Selection sort does not have a no-change stop rule.
An empty or one-item list is already sorted. Duplicate and negative values work. This version changes the original list.
Selection sort is not generally stable. A long swap can move one tied item past another. For example, swapping 1 with 2A in [2A, 2B, 1] leaves [1, 2B, 2A]. The letters label equal values.
How much work and extra room?
With n items, the scans make (n - 1) + (n - 2) + ... + 1 comparisons. Both already sorted and badly mixed input take O(n²) time because every scan still happens.
There are at most n - 1 swap steps. A few positions and one temporary value use O(1) extra space. Few swaps do not mean few comparisons.

blocks.title: Try one small change
blocks.text: Change the list to [3, 1, 2]. First select 1 and swap it with 3, giving [1, 3, 2]. Then select 2. Check that the output is 1 2 3.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Set smallest = start at the beginning of each pass. Reusing the previous smallest position can pull an item out of the part you already finished.
